How WebGPU changes graphics on the web

By Ada Lovelace

WebGPU is a new web standard that gives pages direct, modern access to the graphics card. It replaces much of what WebGL offered with an API designed around how today's GPUs actually work. For developers this means lower overhead, better multithreading and, for the first time on the web, general-purpose compute shaders that run next to rendering.

The specification was developed by a W3C working group with input from every major browser vendor. Chrome shipped it first, and other browsers followed on their own schedules. Because the API maps closely to Vulkan, Metal and Direct3D 12, browsers can translate calls efficiently.

Why compute shaders matter

Compute shaders let a page run massively parallel work on the GPU without drawing anything. Machine learning inference is the headline use: libraries can now run language models in the browser at useful speeds. Physics simulations, image processing and video effects benefit in the same way, since they all apply the same small program to large amounts of data.

Here is the smallest useful setup: request an adapter, then a device.

const adapter = await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter();
const device = await adapter.requestDevice();
console.log(device.limits.maxBufferSize);

Browser support at a glance

BrowserStatus
ChromeShipped
FirefoxPartial

The diagram shows how a command encoder records work that is later submitted to the device queue. Recording and submission are separate steps, which is what makes multithreaded rendering possible: several workers can record command buffers at once and hand them to the queue together.

What to watch out for

Not every device supports WebGPU, and some expose smaller limits than others. Well-behaved pages check for support, fall back gracefully, and ask for only the limits they need. Privacy is another concern: detailed adapter information can be used for fingerprinting, so some browsers deliberately hide it.
